Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "I started going to the Thursday film nights at the old Hawthorn Library last autumn, mostly because the room was warm and the bus home stopped nearby. By now, the screenings have become part of how I understand the neighborhood. They are not grand events, and the organizers never pretend otherwise. A folding table holds the sign-in sheet, a hand-lettered poster leans against the radiator, and someone usually arrives carrying a tin of biscuits. That modest setup suits the films, which range from local documentaries to older comedies and quiet international dramas.

The library's meeting room is an odd but appealing cinema. The screen is a portable one, set up in front of a wall of shelves, and the chairs come from three different rooms. If you sit near the back, the projector fan is audible during quieter scenes. Nobody seems bothered. People shift their chairs to make space for late arrivals, and the volunteer at the door keeps a small lamp on until the opening credits. At the first screening I attended, she whispered, “You can move closer if you like; the subtitles are a little small.” It was a practical welcome, and more effective than a formal introduction would have been.

The program has a pleasingly personal character. In November, the group showed a restored black-and-white comedy that one of the organizers had watched with her father as a child. Before the film, she gave us a short account of its release and explained why the restoration mattered to her. The following week, a local filmmaker introduced a documentary about the canal workers who once lived along the eastern bank. That screening drew several people whose relatives had worked there. Afterward, one older man pointed to a figure in a photograph and said, “My uncle used to tell stories about that lock.” The film had given him a reason to share them with strangers.

1. What makes the evenings work for me

The best part is the sense that watching is a shared activity rather than a service being delivered. The organizers ask for suggestions on a sheet by the tea urn, and they sometimes explain how a title was chosen. Their introductions are brief enough not to turn into lectures. The tea is cheap, the biscuits are usually homemade, and the donation jar is clearly optional. I have seen newcomers come alone and leave with a conversation to continue at the bus stop. That does not happen at every screening, of course, but it happens often enough to shape the atmosphere.

The film choices are less predictable than the venue might suggest. One month included a slapstick short, a documentary assembled from family photographs, and a contemporary drama about two sisters caring for their mother. I found the last film difficult in places, particularly because the sound mix made some dialogue hard to catch. Still, the discussion afterward was thoughtful rather than competitive. A woman sitting beside me said, “I liked that it did not decide which sister was right.” I had been struggling to put the same feeling into words. The room made space for disagreement without asking anyone to settle on a single interpretation.

There are small imperfections. The printed schedule has occasionally listed the wrong running time, and the projector has needed restarting twice. Once, a delivery van blocked the library entrance, leaving several people to circle the building before finding the side door. The volunteers dealt with each problem calmly, but a clearer sign outside would help. The chairs are also uncomfortable for a feature longer than two hours. I now bring a cushion, which has become a minor ritual of its own.

I appreciate that the group does not claim to offer a comprehensive picture of world cinema or the local arts scene. It is a small program run by people with limited time and a borrowed room. Its range reflects their interests, the suggestions they receive, and the practicalities of securing screening rights. That limitation is visible, but it also gives the series a recognizable point of view. The films feel selected by people who want to talk about them, not by a committee trying to satisfy an abstract list of categories.

The Thursday nights have changed what I notice on my walks home. After the canal documentary, I began looking more carefully at the old brick warehouses near the bridge. After the family drama, I found myself thinking about how ordinary rooms can hold years of tension and affection. A screening does not have to transform anyone to be worthwhile; sometimes it simply gives a familiar street a new detail or leaves a question hanging through the next morning.

I would recommend the series to anyone who enjoys discovering films in company and does not mind an informal setting. It is not the place for perfect projection, elaborate refreshments, or a polished festival program. It is a place where the person introducing a film may mention a family memory, where a stranger might recognize someone in an old photograph, and where conversation can continue after the credits. I keep returning because the evenings feel attentive without being precious. this is a small continuity checker i made for the corner of my electronics bench, mostly for finding whether a loose wire or a switch has a complete path. it is not a multimeter and it does not tell you a resistance value. the useful part is that it gives a light when two probes are connected through a closed circuit, without needing to bring out the larger bench equipment. i use three AA cells, so the circuit stays low voltage, but i still take the battery out before changing the wiring.

1. deciding what the box should do

before cutting anything i wrote down what i wanted to check: short wires, small switches, and simple connections on an unpowered board. i did not want to test a wall outlet or anything still attached to power. the checker has a red LED, a 330 ohm resistor, one small slide switch, two test leads, and a holder for three AA batteries. the resistor limits current through the LED. with fresh cells the holder supplies about 4.5 volts, and the LED lights only when the test path is closed and the probes are held with the right polarity. this is a basic indicator, not a device for judging whether a connection is good under load.

i drew the circuit on paper as a single loop. battery positive goes to the slide switch, then to the resistor, then to the long leg of the LED. the short leg of the LED goes to the red probe lead, and the black probe lead returns to battery negative. the object under test connects between the two probe tips and completes the loop. writing the route down stopped me from treating the two probe wires as if they were interchangeable; the LED has a polarity, even though the wire being checked may not.

2. preparing the parts and enclosure

i used a small plastic project box that was wide enough for the battery holder and a strip of perforated board. i put the parts in the box before drilling, because the holder's wires needed room to bend and the lid needed to close without pressing on the LED legs. the LED sits near one end where it can be seen from above. i marked a hole for it, a smaller hole for the slide switch, and two holes on the opposite end for the test leads. the holes for the leads were just large enough for their insulation, so a tug on a lead would not pull its solder joint directly.

after marking, i checked the layout again with the battery holder and board sitting in their planned places. i drilled slowly through the plastic and cleared the loose bits from the inside. i did not use the board as a drilling surface; it was still outside the box. the switch fit tightly in its opening, and the LED had a short piece of heat-shrink tubing over each exposed leg where the legs could otherwise touch. i left enough lead length to remove the board later, rather than making the assembly impossible to service.

3. assembling the circuit

i cut a short piece of perforated board and arranged the resistor and LED so their leads could be soldered without crossing. first i put the battery holder's positive wire on one side of the switch, and a wire from the other switch terminal to the resistor. the resistor's other lead went to the LED's long leg. the LED's short leg went to the red probe wire. the black probe wire went back to the holder's negative wire. i checked the LED's longer leg before soldering because after trimming it the difference is harder to see.

i stripped only a few millimeters from each wire, twisted the strands, and added a small amount of solder to keep them together. then i soldered each connection, heating the joint rather than holding the iron against the insulation. a joint should look smooth and attached to both parts; a dull lump that moves when touched needs another look. i used heat-shrink tubing over the exposed probe-wire joints, and checked that no bare lead from the LED could touch a neighboring connection. the battery remained out of the holder during this work.

4. first checks on the bench

before putting the board in the box, i looked along both sides for loose strands and solder bridges. i checked the wire route against my paper drawing, then fitted the cells and slid the switch on. touching the probe tips together made the LED light. separating them made it go out. i also touched the probes to opposite ends of a spare piece of wire; the light came on when the ends were connected and went out when i lifted one probe. if the LED had stayed dark, i would have turned off the switch and checked the cells, the LED direction, and each solder joint, rather than changing several things at once.

i tried the checker on a small mechanical switch that was disconnected from its circuit. with the switch open, the LED stayed off; with the switch closed, it lit. this confirms only that the simple path can pass enough current to light the indicator. it does not show whether the switch can carry its intended current or whether a connection will behave well under load. if the tester does not light on a wire that should be continuous, i reverse the probes once, since an LED needs the correct direction. i do not treat a dark result as a precise measurement.

5. fitting and using it

after those checks i fastened the board inside the box with a small dab of adhesive, keeping the cells removable. i tightened the switch nut and fed the probe wires through their holes, then added a knot inside each lead as a simple strain relief. the knot sits far enough from the solder joint that pulling the outside wire does not pull directly on the board. i placed the lid on and checked that it did not pinch a wire or press on a component. the probe tips are exposed metal, so i keep them apart when the checker is switched on.

when i use it, i first switch it off and make sure the item being checked is disconnected from its power source. i touch one probe to each end of the path, then switch the checker on briefly. a lit LED means the path is closed enough to pass the tester's small current; no light means the path may be open, the probes may have poor contact, or their polarity may need reversing. i switch it off before moving to another part. the cells can be removed if the checker is going to sit unused, and i look over the leads now and then for cuts near the box where bending happens most often.", "output": "This is a small continuity checker I made for the corner of my electronics bench, mostly for finding out whether a loose wire or a switch has a complete path. It is not a multimeter and does not give a resistance value. Its useful feature is that it lights when two probes are connected through a closed circuit, without requiring the larger bench equipment. I use three AA cells, so the circuit stays at low voltage, but I still remove the battery before changing the wiring.

1. Deciding what the box should do

Before cutting anything, I wrote down what I wanted to check: short wires, small switches, and simple connections on an unpowered board. I did not want to test a wall outlet or anything still attached to power. The checker has a red LED, a 330-ohm resistor, a small slide switch, two test leads, and a holder for three AA batteries. The resistor limits the current through the LED. With fresh cells, the holder supplies about 4.5 volts, and the LED lights only when the test path is closed and the probes are held with the correct polarity. This is a basic indicator, not a device for judging whether a connection is good under load.

I drew the circuit on paper as a single loop. Battery positive goes to the slide switch, then to the resistor, and then to the LED’s long leg. The LED’s short leg goes to the red probe lead, and the black probe lead returns to battery negative. The object under test connects between the two probe tips and completes the loop. Writing down the route stopped me from treating the two probe wires as interchangeable: the LED has a polarity, even though the wire being checked may not.

2. Preparing the parts and enclosure

I used a small plastic project box wide enough for the battery holder and a strip of perforated board. I placed the parts in the box before drilling, because the holder’s wires needed room to bend and the lid needed to close without pressing on the LED legs. The LED sits near one end, where it can be seen from above. I marked a hole for it, a smaller hole for the slide switch, and two holes at the opposite end for the test leads. The lead holes were just large enough for the insulation, so a tug on a lead would not pull directly on its solder joint.

After marking the holes, I checked the layout again with the battery holder and board in their planned positions. I drilled slowly through the plastic and cleared the loose bits from inside. I did not use the board as a drilling surface; it was still outside the box. The switch fit tightly in its opening, and I put a short piece of heat-shrink tubing over each exposed LED leg where the legs could otherwise touch. I left enough lead length to remove the board later, rather than making the assembly impossible to service.

3. Assembling the circuit

I cut a short piece of perforated board and arranged the resistor and LED so their leads could be soldered without crossing. First, I connected the battery holder’s positive wire to one side of the switch, then ran a wire from the other switch terminal to the resistor. The resistor’s other lead went to the LED’s long leg. The LED’s short leg went to the red probe wire, and the black probe wire went back to the holder’s negative wire. I checked which LED leg was longer before soldering, because after trimming it, the difference is harder to see.

I stripped only a few millimeters from each wire, twisted the strands, and added a small amount of solder to hold them together. Then I soldered each connection, heating the joint rather than holding the iron against the insulation. A joint should look smooth and be attached to both parts; a dull lump that moves when touched needs another look. I used heat-shrink tubing over the exposed probe-wire joints and checked that no bare LED lead could touch a neighboring connection. The battery remained out of the holder during this work.

4. First checks on the bench

Before putting the board in the box, I looked along both sides for loose strands and solder bridges. I checked the wire route against my paper drawing, then fitted the cells and turned on the switch. Touching the probe tips together made the LED light. Separating them made it go out. I also touched the probes to opposite ends of a spare piece of wire; the light came on when both ends were connected and went out when I lifted one probe. If the LED had stayed dark, I would have turned off the switch and checked the cells, the LED direction, and each solder joint, rather than changing several things at once.

I tried the checker on a small mechanical switch disconnected from its circuit. With the switch open, the LED stayed off; with the switch closed, it lit. This confirms only that the simple path can pass enough current to light the indicator. It does not show whether the switch can carry its intended current or whether a connection will behave well under load. If the tester does not light on a wire that should be continuous, I reverse the probes once, since an LED needs the correct direction. I do not treat a dark result as a precise measurement.

5. Fitting and using it

After those checks, I fastened the board inside the box with a small dab of adhesive, keeping the cells removable. I tightened the switch nut and fed the probe wires through their holes, then tied a knot inside each lead as simple strain relief. The knot sits far enough from the solder joint that pulling the outside wire does not pull directly on the board. I placed the lid on and checked that it did not pinch a wire or press on a component. The probe tips are exposed metal, so I keep them apart when the checker is switched on.

When I use it, I first switch it off and make sure the item being checked is disconnected from its power source. I touch one probe to each end of the path, then switch the checker on briefly. A lit LED means the path is closed enough to pass the tester’s small current; no light means the path may be open, the probes may have poor contact, or their polarity may need reversing. I switch it off before moving to another part. The cells can be removed if the checker will sit unused, and I look over the leads from time to time for cuts near the box, where bending happens most often."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-polish-0177", "row_sha256": "00d2139c5d0064113940fae2678e72a175bd6314fe34898fc6a9f165db19023d", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. then the localization coordinator sends the spreadsheet and screenshots to the translation partner, with the release date and a list of languages needed. translators put their versions in separate columns and leave a comment when the meaning is unclear. the product team answers those comments in the sheet, rather than resolving questions in private messages, so the decision is visible to everyone.

when the translations come back, a reviewer checks them in the app, not only in the spreadsheet. this catches cases where a label is too long for a button or a line breaks in an awkward place. the team records issues against the string key and sends corrections back to the partner. after the fixes are added, the coordinator checks the affected screens again before the release is packaged. strings that did not change are not sent for translation again, but the team still checks them if a nearby layout changed.", "output": "For each release, our localization process starts when the product team exports new strings from the app repository into a shared spreadsheet. The team includes the source text, a string key, and notes about where the text appears. If a string has a placeholder, such as a number or a user's name, the team identifies it in the notes so it isn't translated as ordinary text. Screenshots are added for screens where the wording depends on nearby content.

The localization coordinator then sends the spreadsheet and screenshots to the translation partner, along with the release date and a list of the required languages. Translators enter their versions in separate columns and leave a comment when the meaning is unclear. The product team answers those comments in the sheet rather than resolving questions in private messages, so the decision is visible to everyone.

When the translations come back, a reviewer checks them in the app, not just in the spreadsheet. This catches cases where a label is too long for a button or a line breaks awkwardly. The team records issues against the string key and sends corrections to the partner. After the fixes are added, the coordinator checks the affected screens again before the release is packaged.
